summary: You produced a correct brute-force solution that passed all visible tests, but it failed one hidden test due to performance constraints. The biggest gap was complexity reasoning: the implementation is O(n^2) and the interview discussion asserted it was O(n), which would be a serious signal in a real interview.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed; one hidden test likely timed out due to quadratic runtime.

dimensions.what_to_improve: Meet the stated large-input constraint: the current approach does not complete within time limits on worst-case inputs. Implement the hash-map single-pass approach so correctness holds under performance requirements.

dimensions.what_to_improve: When constraints explicitly warn that O(n^2) will time out, treat the brute-force as a stepping stone and immediately pivot to an O(n) strategy (hash map / complement lookup) before declaring the solution optimal.

dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: Space usage is indeed O(1) for the brute-force implementation, and the early return can help average-case runtime on some distributions.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Adopt the canonical optimal approach from the answer key: single pass + hash map of value->index to achieve O(n) time. Also calibrate your complexity claims against actual loop structure; an inner loop per i makes total work quadratic.

dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is short, readable, and avoids off-by-one issues by using range(i + 1, len(nums)). Early return is clear and correct.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Remove unnecessary guards that contradict constraints (e.g., `if not nums`) unless the interface truly requires it, and align return behavior with typical expectations (e.g., always returning a pair since one is guaranteed) or document deviations.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: Completed an initial working solution without hints and passed the full visible suite.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independently incorporate constraint-driven optimization without prompting—here, despite an explicit warning about O(n^2), the solution stayed quadratic and was asserted to be optimal.

thinking_and_logic: The implemented approach checks every pair (i, j) with i < j and returns as soon as it finds a pair summing to target. While this is logically straightforward and correct for many cases, it scales poorly because it performs up to ~n(n-1)/2 checks. The interview discussion also mischaracterized this as O(n), which conflicts with both the code structure and the stated constraints warning about timeouts.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key's brute-force solution (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space). The canonical optimal solution you missed is the single-pass hash map (value->index) approach: for each number x at index i, check whether target-x is already in the map; if so return those indices, otherwise store x. That technique reduces runtime to O(n) and is the expected solution under the given constraints; your current code cannot guarantee passing the largest hidden case.

next_steps.action: Re-implement Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (complement lookup before insert).
next_steps.why: It is the canonical optimal approach and satisfies the O(n) time requirement that your current solution violates.
next_steps.how: Maintain a dict seen: value->index. For each i, x=nums[i], if (target-x) in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; else seen[x]=i.

next_steps.action: Practice complexity explanations for common loop patterns (nested loops, two pointers, hash lookups).
next_steps.why: The incorrect O(n) claim on an O(n^2) implementation is a major interview risk even if the code works on small tests.
next_steps.how: For each solution you write, compute the number of iterations symbolically (e.g., sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (n-i-1) = n(n-1)/2) and state time/space explicitly.

next_steps.action: Do 5-10 variants that force choosing the right pattern from constraints (e.g., Two Sum, Subarray Sum Equals K, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters).
next_steps.why: These problems build the habit of mapping constraints to the right tool (hash map / sliding window) instead of stopping at brute force.
next_steps.how: Before coding, write: 'Constraints imply O(n log n) or better; choose pattern X; expected time/space Y' and validate after implementation.

encouragement: You’re close—your baseline implementation is correct and clean; the main unlock is treating constraints as requirements and consistently matching your approach (and complexity explanation) to them.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
